transcript:
Header: 2027-12-11 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~62 minutes | Recording: Yes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Michael Ortiz (Hydra Head of Platform), Leila Khan (Hydra SRE), Benji Park (Hydra ML Eng), Sara Gomez (Hydra Procurement)

Summary: quick kickoff to align on scope for a POC to validate Hydra's fraud scoring inference path under production-like traffic, define benchmarks, and agree timelines and artifacts.

00:00:05 Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, i'll kick us off — quick intro, i'm alex from redwood, priya is our systems engineer who will run the bench.
00:00:14 Michael Ortiz: hey alex, michelle — michael here, thanks. leila, benji, sara on the line. we have a hard project timeline so want to be efficient.
00:00:23 Alex Chen: great. objective for today — figure out the workload characteristics you care about, success criteria, and decide on whether we'll run on hosted or dedicated for the pilot. also define what we need from you for a realistic replay. does that sound right?
00:00:36 Leila Khan: yes, also security questions — we'll need to know about audit logs, key mgmt, and network.
00:00:41 Priya Nair: noted. we'll touch on those. quick context question — benji, can you summarize the current inference path, qps numbers, and prompt size?
00:00:51 Benji Park: sure, so our live scoring endpoint gets bursty traffic — average 120 QPS, peak short bursts up to 2.1k qps during batch processing windows, long-tail during training jobs. concurrency at model level is about 350 concurrent inferences for the real-time lane, sometimes spiking to ~900 for 30s.
00:01:14 Alex Chen: ok that's helpful — when you say tokens, what's the input and output token mix roughly?
00:01:19 Benji Park: input is small — about 12 to 40 tokens average, most at 18. output can be variable because we include explanations sometimes, output avg around 60 tokens, but there's a tail where some explainers go up to 400 tokens.
00:01:34 Priya Nair: that tail is important — KV cache and prefix reuse can help on repeated prompts but for unique explainers caching is less effective.
00:01:44 Michael Ortiz: that's our pain point — cost and tail latency on those explainer requests. we need p95 under 200ms for business-critical scoring and p99 under 450ms ideally. cost target is to keep incremental token cost below $X per million tokens — we'll confirm exact number with finance.
00:01:58 Sara Gomez: procurement will need a cost estimate and a rough commitment for dedicated capacity if that looks necessary.
00:02:06 Alex Chen: understood. broadly, we propose a two-phase POC: 1) workload characterization — get sample traffic, run replay on a small fleet to map QPS->latency and token-cost; 2) focused benchmark — run a few 4-hour windows at target peak shapes to validate p50/p95/p99 and throughput. Does two-phase make sense?
00:02:25 Leila Khan: yes, and we want to test both hosted and privately deployed configurations — to see if network/VPC egress changes latency.
00:02:33 Priya Nair: we can do hosted first to move fast, then a private VPC deployment for apples-to-apples. note that private will require a little setup time for VPC peering or VPN and KMS integration.
00:02:45 Benji Park: how do you recommend we capture token distribution? we have logs but they're anonymized.
00:02:51 Alex Chen: best is a 48-hour sample trace with per-request metadata: timestamp, request size tokens in, response tokens out, model variant, and a flag for explanation vs short-score. we don't need PII, so you can hash IDs. that replay input lets us build the token histogram and time-of-day burst map.
00:03:09 Michael Ortiz: timeline wise, we want results before the end of the year — is that feasible?
00:03:15 Priya Nair: tight but feasible if we get data quickly; our earliest benchmark window would be week of 2027-12-20. we can run a smaller smoke replay earlier to sanity-check.
00:03:25 Sara Gomez: procurement needs commercial terms; we will also evaluate whether a reserved pool makes sense.
00:03:31 Alex Chen: i'll send a preliminary cost model and two commercial options: pay-as-you-go hosted and a 3-month reserved for dedicated.
00:03:40 Leila Khan: wanted to call out SLOs — p95 under 200ms for regular scoring, p99 under 450ms, and tail like p99.9 we'd like under 1s but that's aspirational.
00:03:52 Priya Nair: we should also capture cold-start effects for rare model variants, and note tokenization differences across model families — sometimes tokenizer mismatches cause token counts to be off.
00:04:05 Benji Park: we use a small custom ensemble — main model plus a short-circuit micro-model for quick negative scoring; we'll provide flags in the logs.
00:04:14 Alex Chen: perfect. for benchmark metrics we'll collect: p50/p95/p99/p99.9 latencies, throughput achieved, GPU utilization, per-token compute cost, and correctness regressions vs your golden set. any other metrics?
00:04:27 Michael Ortiz: need detailed error traces and tracer ids to map failures to customer requests.
00:04:31 Priya Nair: we'll include distributed tracing hooks and correlation IDs in the runbook.
00:04:36 Leila Khan: about safety and compliance — do you support customer-managed KMS and audit logs for private?
00:04:42 Alex Chen: yes, private supports bring-your-own-key and audit logs; hosted can integrate with customer KMS for certain enterprise tiers. we'll attach our security pack.
00:04:51 Benji Park: for the replay, should we preserve original inter-arrival times or accelerate?
00:04:55 Priya Nair: both. do a time-preserved replay to capture real burst shapes, and an accelerated replay to stress the system and map max throughput. we'll parameterize the replay.
00:05:06 Michael Ortiz: what about model variants — some of our traffic hits a quantized faster model for cost reasons, some call the full float model.
00:05:12 Alex Chen: include model_variant field in the trace. we'll run the same mix during benchmarks and also run a worst-case where all requests go to the heaviest model.
00:05:19 Leila Khan: what if the hosted runs show p95 near limit — is there automatic fallback/graded degradation?
00:05:25 Priya Nair: yes, Redwood runtime supports routing rules — fallback to cheaper model variants, region-fallback, and graceful queuing; we can simulate those during the test.
00:05:34 Benji Park: can we get sample dashboards for the metrics you collect?
00:05:38 Alex Chen: we'll share a sample dashboard and the benchmark template.
00:05:42 Michael Ortiz: great. on security docs — we'll need SOC2 docs and network diagrams for our security team.
00:05:47 Alex Chen: will attach security pack and a blank SOC2 questionnaire.
00:05:50 Sara Gomez: about procurement, what are lead times for dedicated?
00:05:54 Alex Chen: for dedicated, after contract signing, typical provisioning is 2-4 weeks depending on capacity and region. for the pilot we often do a small reserved pool to validate throughput.
00:06:05 Leila Khan: ok, risk appetite — we can tolerate a short pilot with hosted but production will likely want private.
00:06:10 Priya Nair: to be explicit on success criteria — we propose: 1) p95 < 200ms for 95% of test windows; 2) p99 < 450ms for 90% of test windows; 3) cost per 1M user tokens within your target +/-20%; and 4) no functional regressions on the golden prompt set. happy to formalize.
00:06:28 Michael Ortiz: that matches our expectations; let's add acceptance of a rollback plan if regressions exceed thresholds.
00:06:34 Alex Chen: sounds fair. next, logistics for data — benji, can you confirm what format you can export?
00:06:40 Benji Park: we can export JSON lines with fields, but timestamps are epoch ms. we'll scrub PII and add a model_variant tag.
00:06:47 Priya Nair: that's perfect. please also include a small sample (1000 requests) so we can pre-validate the parser.
00:06:54 Benji Park: will do.
00:06:57 Michael Ortiz: any concerns about rate-limiting or throttles on your side during the replay?
00:07:02 Priya Nair: we have controls; we'll coordinate the window. for the accelerated stress test we may recommend running from our internal runner to avoid client-side rate limits.
00:07:12 Leila Khan: what about measuring cold-starts per pod/instance?
00:07:16 Priya Nair: we can instrument warmup traces and measure first-token latency per cold-start; include flags to simulate scale-up vs warm cache.
00:07:26 Alex Chen: ok, so immediate deliverables from redwood: benchmark spec, replay tooling link, sample dashboard, security pack, and cost model. from hydra: 48h trace, sample of 1k events, list of golden prompts, and procurement contacts.
00:07:40 Sara Gomez: procurement will circle back with timing for commercial evaluation.
00:07:44 Michael Ortiz: one more — we want to validate tail-latency under 30-second sustained bursts not just short blips.
00:07:51 Priya Nair: we'll include a long-burst test profile in the runbook.
00:07:55 Alex Chen: good. anything else?
00:07:58 Benji Park: curious about quantization suggestions — do you provide recommended configs per workload?
00:08:02 Priya Nair: yes, Optimize will give model/quantization recommendations and expected perf/cost delta; we'll run a couple of quantized variants during the benchmarks.
00:08:12 Leila Khan: can you also test queuing behaviors — how your autoscaler and request batching work under burst?
00:08:18 Priya Nair: yes, we'll capture queue length, batch sizes, and the effect on latencies.
00:08:24 Alex Chen: ok let's recap action items and timelines — i'll send the deck and the cost model today, priya will post the runbook by 12/14, benji to deliver traces by 12/18, and we aim for a benchmark during week of 12/20. does that reflect the plan?
00:08:38 Michael Ortiz: yes.
00:08:40 Sara Gomez: yes.
00:08:42 Alex Chen: awesome. thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the calendar invite for the bench window.
00:08:48 Michael Ortiz: thanks all.

[End of meeting]

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-hearings noted (e.g., K-V cache transcribed as K-V cash), some speaker labels normalized.
